Performance measures

Source: vignettes/articles/analysis-performance.Rmd
analysis-performance.Rmd

The performance measures are the numbers used to judge an investment over a period: how much it returned, how bumpy the ride was, how far it fell, and how it did against a benchmark. They are methods on every instrument and on every asset basket, because both supply prices(). They live in the PerformanceMeasures class in R/assets_analysis_performance_measures.R, the last link of the analysis chain, which Instrument and AssetBasket both inherit.

Each method takes the usual range arguments, interval, from_date, to_date, days and adjusted, and works on the closing prices. A return is the fractional change of the close from one candle to the next. Annual figures scale by 252 candles a year for day candles, and by the number of candles in 252 sessions of 375 minutes for a minute interval such as 5minute; any other interval signals ValueError before any request is sent. A risk_free_rate is an annual fraction, so a 6.5 percent treasury bill is 0.065, and it defaults to 0, because a built-in rate would go stale.

The table below lists the measures.

Method What it means A good value
cumulative_return Total growth over the range Higher
annualised_return The compound annual growth rate Higher
annualised_volatility The standard deviation of returns, scaled to a year Lower, for the same return
sharpe_ratio(risk_free_rate) Annual return above the risk-free rate for each unit of volatility Above 1 is usually thought good
sortino_ratio(risk_free_rate) The Sharpe ratio with only the falls counted as risk Higher
drawdowns How far below its earlier peak the close stood at every candle A data frame, not a single number
maximum_drawdown The worst fall from a peak, as a negative fraction Closer to zero
calmar_ratio Annual growth rate divided by the size of the worst drawdown Higher
value_at_risk(confidence, method) The one-candle loss not exceeded on that share of candles, "historical" or "parametric" Lower
expected_shortfall(confidence) The average loss on the candles beyond the value at risk Lower
benchmark_beta(benchmark) How much the price moved for each percent the benchmark moved 1 moves with the market
alpha(benchmark, risk_free_rate) Annual return beyond what the beta explains, Jensen’s alpha Positive
tracking_error(benchmark) Annual volatility of the return difference from the benchmark Near zero for an index fund
information_ratio(benchmark) Annual return above the benchmark for each unit of tracking error Higher
up_capture_ratio(benchmark), down_capture_ratio(benchmark) How much of the benchmark’s rises and falls were captured Up above 1, down below 1
performance_summary(benchmark = NULL, ...) Every measure above from one fetch of the candles A named list

A benchmark is anything with a prices() method, so an instrument can be measured against an index, a basket against the index it copies, or one fund’s holdings against another’s.

The R methods follow the Python library’s pandas calls exactly. Standard deviations, variances and covariances divide by n - 1, as pandas does; quantiles use linear interpolation, stats::quantile(type = 7); the parametric value at risk uses stats::qnorm(); and the running peak behind drawdowns() skips missing values, as pandas’ cummax() does, where base R’s cummax() would turn everything after a missing value into NA. On 2026-10-07 every measure was compared with the Python class on the same fixture candles, with risk-free rates of 0 and 0.065, day and 5minute intervals, three confidence levels and both value at risk methods, and the largest relative difference was 3.8e-15.

Example

The example below measures INFY against NIFTY over a year.

infosys <- Equity$new(exchange = "nse", symbol = "INFY")
nifty <- EquityIndex$new(exchange = "nse", symbol = "NIFTY")
summary <- infosys$performance_summary(
  benchmark = nifty,
  risk_free_rate = 0.065,
  days = 365
)
str(summary)

performance_summary() returns a named list, where the Python library returns a pandas Series. Its names are always the same nine, or fifteen with a benchmark, in the order of the table above: cumulative_return, annualised_return, annualised_volatility, sharpe_ratio, sortino_ratio, maximum_drawdown, calmar_ratio, value_at_risk and expected_shortfall, followed by benchmark_beta, alpha, tracking_error, information_ratio, up_capture_ratio and down_capture_ratio. A measure that cannot be calculated is a NULL element that stays in the list, so summary[["sharpe_ratio"]] always works. It fetches the candles once for the instrument and once for the benchmark.

When the Python library ran the same summary on 2026-09-28, INFY’s Sharpe ratio over the year was -1.302082 and its maximum drawdown was -0.416913, and both matched a separate calculation with pandas to every printed digit. Its beta against NIFTY was 0.684382, with an up capture ratio of 0.596877 and a down capture ratio of 0.963832.

A mutual fund returns NULL for every measure, because UBI stores no candles or net asset value for one; measure its constituents instead.
